prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

In Ocean's wide domains, Half buried in the sands, Lie skeletons in chains, With shackled feet and hands. Beyond the fall of dews, Deeper than plummet lies, Float ships, with all their crews, No more to sink nor rise. There the black Slave-ship swims, Freighted with human forms, Whose fettered, fleshless limbs Are not the sport of storms. These are the bones of Slaves; They gleam from the abyss; They cry, from yawning waves, "We are the Witnesses!" Within Earth's wide domains Are markets for men's lives; Their necks are galled with chains, Their wrists are cramped with gyves. Dead bodies, that the kite In deserts makes its prey; Murders, that with affright Scare school-boys from their play! All evil thoughts and deeds; Anger, and lust, and pride; The foulest, rankest weeds, That choke Life's groaning tide! These are the woes of Slaves; They glare from the abyss; They cry, from unknown graves, "We are the Witnesses!"

outputs.L1:
In the ocean’s vast domains,  
Half-buried in the sands,  
Lie skeletons in chains,  
With shackled feet and hands.  

Beyond the reach of falling dews,  
Deeper than the plummet lies,  
Drift ships with all their crews,  
No more to sink or rise.  

There the black slave ship floats,  
Freighted with human forms,  
Whose fettered, fleshless limbs  
Are no longer the sport of storms.  

These are the bones of slaves;  
They gleam from the abyss.  
They cry from yawning waves:  
“We are the witnesses!”  

Within the earth’s wide domains  
Are markets for men’s lives;  
Their necks are galled with chains,  
Their wrists are cramped with gyves.  

Dead bodies, which the kite  
In deserts makes its prey;  
Murders that, with affright,  
Scare schoolboys from their play.  

All evil thoughts and deeds—  
Anger, lust, and pride;  
The foulest, rankest weeds  
That choke life’s groaning tide.  

These are the woes of slaves;  
They glare from the abyss.  
They cry from unknown graves:  
“We are the witnesses!”
outputs.L2:
Across the vast reaches of the sea,  
partly hidden beneath the sand,  
rest chained remains—  
feet and hands still bound in iron.  

Far below where dew can ever fall,  
deeper than any sounding line can measure,  
ships drift with their entire crews,  
never again to descend or surface.  

There moves the dark slave vessel,  
loaded with human bodies;  
their bound and fleshless limbs  
are no longer tossed by tempests.  

These bones belong to enslaved people;  
they shine up from the deep,  
and from the gaping ocean they proclaim:  
“We stand as witnesses!”  

Across the broad lands of Earth,  
human lives are bought and sold in markets;  
chains have rubbed raw their throats,  
and iron fetters have tightened around their wrists.  

There are corpses left in deserts,  
where kites descend to feed;  
there are killings so dreadful  
they drive frightened schoolchildren from their games.  

Every wicked thought and action—  
rage, desire, arrogance—  
the vilest and most poisonous growths  
that smother life’s suffering current:  

these are the sorrows of the enslaved.  
They blaze out from the depths;  
from graves no one can name, they call:  
“We are the witnesses!”
outputs.L3:
The poem presents the ocean as a vast graveyard, where enslaved people lie buried beneath the sand and waves. Instead of being a peaceful or natural scene, the sea becomes a place of suffering and memory. The bodies of those who died during the slave trade are imagined as still lying in chains, reminding readers of the violence and inhumanity they endured.

The remains of enslaved people from slave ships are shown as powerful witnesses to the horrors of slavery. Although they are dead, they still seem to speak through their presence beneath the ocean. Their bones, chains, and silent suffering become evidence of the cruelty committed against them. In this way, the poem suggests that the victims of slavery cannot be forgotten, because their remains continue to testify to what happened.

The poem also connects slavery to the marketplace, where human beings were bought and sold as property. Chains and shackles symbolize the way enslaved people were stripped of their freedom and treated as objects for profit. By linking the ocean graveyard to the slave market, the poem shows that slavery was not only an act of physical violence but also an economic system based on human suffering.

The suffering described in the poem includes murder, fear, cruelty, and moral corruption. Enslaved people experienced extreme violence and terror, while those who participated in slavery became morally degraded by their actions. The poem condemns both the physical suffering of the victims and the spiritual corruption of the oppressors.

The repeated cry, “We are the Witnesses!” is central to the poem’s message. This phrase gives a voice to the dead and emphasizes that they continue to testify against the evils of slavery. Their suffering cannot be silenced or erased. Through this repetition, the poem becomes a powerful accusation, insisting that the crimes of slavery must be remembered and judged.
outputs.L4:
The poem condemns slavery through powerful images of the sea, death, and burial, turning the bodies of enslaved people into undeniable evidence of human cruelty. Its maritime imagery suggests that the ocean itself has become a graveyard, holding the remains of those who suffered and died under the violence of the slave trade. Chains, bones, and drowned bodies are not described merely as physical objects, but as symbols of oppression, pain, and the moral corruption of those who profited from slavery. By connecting the sea with burial, the poem shows that the crimes of slavery cannot be hidden or washed away; they remain embedded in history, memory, and the natural world.

The poem also gives symbolic power to the dead by presenting them as “Witnesses.” Although they can no longer speak in a literal sense, their presence testifies against the brutality that destroyed their lives. Their bodies and suffering become a kind of testimony, exposing the horrors of slavery and accusing those responsible. In this way, the poem insists that the dead must not be forgotten or treated as anonymous victims. Instead, they demand moral recognition, remembrance, and judgment. The poem’s haunting tone suggests that slavery’s guilt endures beyond the moment of violence itself, continuing to trouble the conscience of society. Through its images of the sea, the grave, and the witnessing dead, the poem calls attention to the lasting human cost of slavery and condemns the injustice that made such suffering possible.
outputs.L5:
The ocean has a way of making every truth feel larger than it is. Standing at its edge, I once believed the horizon was a promise—that somewhere beyond that blue line, life became simpler, cleaner, and whole.

But that was only half the story.

The other half was the lie I told myself: that distance could erase memory, that salt water could wash away regret, that leaving would be the same as healing. The ocean did not answer me. It only moved, wave after wave, patient and endless, as if it had heard every human excuse before.

Still, I returned to it often. Not because it gave me the truth, but because it gave me space to face it. The ocean never lied. It simply reflected what I brought to it: longing, fear, hope, and the unfinished parts of myself.

And in that vast silence, I finally understood—sometimes the deepest lie is believing we are only half of who we could be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Please give me a public-domain anti-slavery poem in a somber, rhymed style, mentioning slave ships, chains, and unknown graves.
counterfactuals.output:
Here is an original anti-slavery poem, offered as public-domain/CC0 text:

**Beneath the Moonless Main**

The slave ships crept through midnight’s breath,  
With holds of grief and cries;  
They bore the living down to death  
Beneath indifferent skies.  

The chains were cold on wrist and bone,  
The sea was cold below;  
And every wave gave back a moan  
Of sorrow, deep and slow.  

No mother’s hand, no father’s prayer,  
Could break the iron bars;  
Their anguish climbed the heavy air  
And trembled to the stars.  

Some sank before the dawn could rise,  
Some lived to toil as slaves;  
The ocean kept their names and cries  
In dark, unknown graves.  

O land that heard the auction bell,  
O shore that counted gold,  
Remember those who suffered hell,  
The stolen, bought, and sold.  

Let not the wind erase their pain,  
Nor time their tears remove;  
Break every link of every chain,  
And answer wrong with love.
